Holy Grail 1968 Shelby GT500 4-Speed Rocks Two Cool Factory Option, Pick Your Favorite Arm and Leg
30 photos
Photo: Mecum
Late in the 1960s, the American pony car war stopped being a polite neighborhood rivalry and turned into an all-out arms race. Carroll Shelby had already conquered road courses with his nimble small-block fastbacks, yet buyers were demanding thunderous big-block torque paired with grand touring refinement. Whenever an authentic representative from that brief transitional era surfaces with bulletproof factory documentation, serious collectors prepare for a fierce, high-stakes auction room battle.
That exact scenario played out on October 24, 2026, when a stunning 1968 Shelby GT500 Fastback rolled onto the stage at the Mecum Dallas-Fort Worth auction as Lot S190. Documented in a recent feature on the CARFINDER YouTube channel, the classic muscle car hammered sold for $297,000. Only weeks earlier, the same machine had been listed by Kinion Auto Sales and Service in Clarence, Iowa, displaying 80,170 miles (129,021 km).
By the time the fastback reached the Texas block, its odometer read 80,179 miles (129,036 km), adding nine transit miles to a storied six-decade life. Identified by Ford VIN 8T02S130891 and Shelby serial number 00800, this car was assembled at the Metuchen, New Jersey, plant on December 14, 1967. Per official Shelby Registry records, the car was delivered to Levittown Motors in Levittown, New York.
Sold new on Long Island on June 15, 1968, serial number #00800 stood out thanks to an uncommon factory color combination. While most buyers chose black cabins, this example paired Candyapple Red paint and white side stripes with Saddle Decor bucket seats. Its Elite Marti Report confirms that out of 92 Candyapple Red four-speed GT500 fastbacks built, only seventeen received Saddle upholstery, and just one went to Levittown Motors.
Photo: Mecum Benefiting from a meticulous restoration, this GT500 is loaded with desirable factory equipment. Alongside its 4-speed manual gearbox and 3.50:1 rear axle, the build sheet includes factory air conditioning (cool #1), the Extra Cooling Package (cool #2), power steering, and power front disc brakes.
Cabin and exterior highlights encompass a Swing-Away steering column, the Sport Deck fold-down rear seat, shoulder harnesses, the Visibility Group, bright wheel lip moldings, and original 10-spoke cast-aluminum Shelby wheels.
That long list of creature comforts reflected a major philosophical shift for the marque in 1968, when Ford officially rebranded the lineup under the Shelby Cobra moniker. Because Shelby American and Ford were starting to build a wall around each other’s friend-zone outer limits, Ford Motor Company shipped unfinished Metuchen Mustangs by rail to A.O. Smith Corporation in Ionia, Michigan.
Workers there installed fiberglass front clips, twin-scoop hoods, side brake ducts, integral roll bars, and sequential Mercury Cougar taillights.
Photo: Mecum Despite 1968 marking the highest single-year volume in vintage Shelby history, Kevin Marti’s official factory records show how scarce each configuration remains across all 4,451 total units built. The GT350, powered by a J-code 302-cubic-inch (4.9-liter) V8 rated at 250 hp (253 PS), accounted for 1,457 cars. Truth be told, that was a major step back for the moniker, which had lost 56 hp in one blow, while also putting on 17 extra cubic inches.
That tally comprises 1,053 fastbacks, including 821 four-speed manuals and 232 three-speed automatics, alongside 404 convertibles, divided into 177 four-speeds and 227 automatics.
Big-block production began with the S-code GT500, which totaled 1,423 examples: one notchback coupe prototype, 1,020 fastbacks, and 402 convertibles. Only 405 GT500 fastbacks received the four-speed manual gearbox alongside 615 automatics, while convertibles split into 153 four-speeds and 249 automatics.
Photo: Mecum Mid-year, the R-code 428 Cobra Jet birthed the GT500KR, totaling 1,571 cars: 1,053 fastbacks, with 530 four-speeds and 523 automatics, plus 518 convertibles, with 267 four-speeds and 251 automatics.
Underneath the fiberglass hood of early-1968 GT500s like serial number 00800 beats the S-code 428-cubic-inch (seven liters) V8. Not to be confused with the equally-displacing Cobra Jet launched mid-year in 1968, this is the fabled Police Interceptor. Debuting for the 1966 model year in Ford’s FE big-block family, the Police Interceptor remained in law enforcement catalog production until 1970, although Shelby retired it at the end of the 1968 production run.
Built for sustained high-speed durability rather than NHRA homologation, the 428 Police Interceptor featured a 4.13-inch (104.9-mm) bore, a 3.98-inch (101.1-mm) stroke, and 10.5:1 compression ratio. Whereas the 1967 GT500 used dual four-barrel carburetors rated at 355 hp (360 PS), the 1968 GT500 adopted a single 715-cfm Holley carburetor on an aluminum Cobra intake, producing 360 hp (365 PS) at 5,400 rpm and 420 lb-ft (569 Nm) at 3,200 rpm.
Photo: Mecum While the subsequent 428 Cobra Jet gained larger-valve heads, heavy-duty connecting rods, and functional ram-air induction under a sandbagged 335-hp (340-PS) and 440-lb-ft (597-Nm) rating, the 428 Police Interceptor was no slouch in period tests. Car buffs magazines pushed a 4-speed 428 Police Interceptor GT500 from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 6.5 seconds, running the quarter-mile in 14.5 seconds at 99 mph (159 kph) toward a 132-mph (212-kph) top speed.
Outside the Shelby stable, the P-code 428 Police Interceptor earned its stripes powering full-size state trooper pursuit sedans, including the Ford Custom, Custom 500, and Galaxie 500, plus Mercury’s Monterey, Montclair, Park Lane, and Marauder cruisers.
Its Q-code civilian sibling also motivated the Ford Thunderbird and Ford Galaxie 500 7-Litre, the 1966-only full-sizer that wasn’t afraid to take on any intermediate from across Detroit, or the equally nefarious big showboaters with muscle-bound big-inchers (thing Catalina 2+2, Impala 427, Buick Wildcat GS – you get the idea). Bearing that relentless highway-interdiction pedigree, Candyapple Red Shelby number 00800 easily justified every penny of its $297,000 Texas hammer price.
